prompt: Objective: set a price for a new software add-on. What you've learned: the add-on saves a typical customer about $5,000 a year. Latest finding: competitors' similar tools cost $1,200–2,000 a year. What is the best next step?

options.text: Ask the interviewer which price the client has in mind
options.feedback: Drive the case: propose the next analysis instead of waiting for a number.

options.text: Estimate the cost to deliver the add-on, to set a price floor
options.feedback: For software, delivery costs almost nothing, so a cost floor barely constrains the price.

options.text: Calculate revenue if the add-on were priced at $5,000
options.feedback: That jumps to a price before understanding why rivals charge far less.

options.text: Learn why rivals charge $1,200–2,000 for $5,000 of value
options.feedback: Right. The gap between value and market prices is the puzzle: features, switching costs or how buyers compare. It shows how much value the client can capture.

explanation: The add-on saves $5,000 a year but rivals charge $1,200–2,000. Understanding that gap shows how much value the client can capture. Software costs little to deliver, so a cost floor matters little.
